transcripts.text: Stories from around the corner and around the country. You're listening to All The Best. Proudly supported by the Art Gallery of New South Wales. You're listening to All The Best from FBi Radio 94.5. I'm Gabriella Accaria. One of my very first jobs was being a bra fitter. It was a very vulnerable role, fitting young women in their very first bras, women who had lost weight, gained weight and women with mastectomies. it's such a challenge for women to find something that fits so it felt like I was doing less of a job and more like I was making them feel comfortable within themselves. So this week we go to work, we hear someone reminisce about a hectic job, an unlikely career pathway, someone finding their voice and that moment where there was a bright spark and I want to start by acknowledging that I'm recording from stolen and Gadigal land and I pay my respects to Gadigal elders past and present. I also recognize that the area where FBI radio is situated, Redfin, has long been a place of storytelling, strength, resistance and resilience for First Nations communities. I think my craziest story from bra fitting was when a 90 year old woman came in. She started fainting in the change room when I was trying to fit her and then after replenishing with some water and sugar she was absolutely insistent that we keep going with the bra fitting. A week later she came in with a gift chocolates and a card thanking me for my service. I've officially retired from retail now though and I love what I do for work. I've always felt the charm of having jumped around jobs a lot and when that charm wears off it can be a very jarring experience. Imagine you've traveled back to the prime time of the 70s, 1975. The latest trend is afros and bell bottoms, hippies are honking their horns of their minibands and their moustaches are bushier than ever. You're heading down to the local roller rink with your best mate when he suddenly turns to you and says I'm moving to Europe to drive buses on group tours. Enter Derek. Today he's 76 and lives in Melbourne but 50 years ago Derek found himself in this exact situation. A young man in London about to take a massive gamble on a company that changed his life forever. Contiki. One of the most interesting jobs that I've had in my career to date was when I and a friend of mine went over to the UK in 1974 and he came up with the idea that of working in Europe as a driver for a camping tour company and I said that's very that's all very good but I was quite happy with my job at the time. And when he came back, he decided to become a driver. He wrote to me whilst he was away. And then he said, why don't I apply? And I said, well, you've just done your training trip. It didn't take much convincing for Derek to sign up. He interviewed for the job that week and got it on the spot. And so on the Friday night of that week, I flew out to Barcelona, where the tour had actually got to in that time. And I got to the camping ground, La Bolina Alegre, it was called, the Laughing Whale in Barcelona. And it was totally in darkness. There were one or two people moving around, but it was at midnight. So I couldn't find anyone. Eventually, he did track down his mate Gary. He set up a tent and met the passengers the next morning to start off his training. On day four, the tour was headed to the Antibes on the French Riviera when they decided to stop for an early lunch. It was a glorious day, I can remember, and we decided to take an early lunch just north of Barcelona and on the beach and people had cozies and they all got into their cozies and I unfortunately ran to the water, as you do, dived in and there was a ridge of rocks underneath the surface of the water and I had my hands out to dive in but the strength of my arms then crushed my head into the water and I was dragged out bleeding. There was an English couple that had a holiday home on the beach, sort of a shack, but they had a small car and they took me to the village where the nearest doctor was and the doctor put seven clamps, like staples, into my head. so that I spent the whole trip then they waited for me whilst I was being tended to I then spent the most of the day lying on the floor of the bus which was a Mercedes Mercedes bus so it was reasonably comfortable but not the floor heading to Auntie. So despite the very warm welcome in the form of a head injury from his first tour there is never any rest for Contiki tour guide because that same evening Derek hopped onto another bus at the Piazza Navona to shadow a whole new experienced crew but the veteran guides had a classic hazing prank brewed up for the new rookie. What I didn't know was my bus my mob they had two really experienced obviously experienced tour leaders and driver because I was trained on it I was being trained on it, decided, which was one of the pranks that they used to pull, to flower bomb the bus. And I, inside this bus, I was absolutely covered in flour and then water. Apart from jumping in the ocean and pulling pranks, being a tour guide back in the 70s was no easy gig. Derek had to carry around $10,000 in physical travellers checks, manage cooking rosters and organised daily meals for over 40 people. He even had a near miss with some horse mints in France after wandering into a butcher shop fiercely decorated with pictures of horse heads on the wall. So now with training completed, the real test begun on his very first solo trip out of London. Day one, the Dover Docks. We got on the ferry to go to Calais and we thought that's great everything's right all of a sudden there was an announcement as the boat left the dock in Dover to say that due to a port strike in France the boat's going to Zeebrugge in Belgium so I had 44 people and a driver on a bus on a ferry not going anywhere near where the bus was I spent the trip in the purser's office talking to my people in England as to what the hell I was going to do. We tread water for a little while, or trod water for a little while, and then about an hour and a half later I got a phone call from the campsite. So, fortunately, this guy then came out to the ferry terminal, picked us up. And after that triple curse, the trip actually went pretty smoothly. Today, these tours are mostly planned on phones and laptops and pretty much everyone knows what's going on. But what was amazing about Derek is that he survived every roadblock on his own, simply with a bit of common sense. P.S. All 44 passengers came out of the trip alive.

From FBi Radio, you're listening to All The Best, proudly supported by the Art Gallery of New South Wales. I'm Gabriella Accaria. That story was from Ellie Starkis, with support from Eleanor Crosby-Hardman and Dylan Bird. Sometimes the wacky thing isn't the job itself. It's the journey that helps you get there. And it takes a little bit of risk-taking and being kind to yourself.

Kerri-Ann didn't start her first real job until she was 26, not because she didn't want to work, because she was already working, at home, raising kids as a single mother. I had had children at a younger age and I stayed at home with them until they were at school, so I didn't really have a lot of experience and it was very hard to get my foot in the door. She ended up getting a few casual jobs, none of which she loved. It wasn't until she studied fitness that she got her first full-time job at a gym, where she stayed for almost a decade. The people were just great there, so motivational. The vibe was great and it was a really, really good job to have. But what she didn't know was that the gym was not her final destination. It was the launching pad for something else. And it all started with a gym chalkboard. There was a gigantic chalkboard which ran from the floor to the roof, which we used to put sales staff up on all the time. So I took it to the manager and I was like, right, it's time for change. We need to do something really cool here. We need to blow members away as they walk through the door. Like something really cool. I think we should do this. I think at the time it was a huge Marvel piece or something and a cool positive quote to go with it. And he turned around and said, yes. I just like talked this right up and now I had to deliver. So the pressure felt like it was on. Kerri-Ann began designing on the gym chalkboard regularly and her designs took off. everyone who came in kept asking who the artist was it got the members attention it didn't even just get the members attention it got the town's attention I had people asking they're like are you that girl who's doing these chalkboards it was absolutely amazing so coming up the ideas for the chalkboard it was a bit of a team effort sometimes it was me I found something cool that I'd like sometimes it was a team effort and people were like oh what about this what about that and then other times it was members who put in requests so it became quite a thing it was quite fun it varied on how long it took to put on the board just because I still did have to work my job at the same time so it depended on how busy we were but generally speaking it took anywhere between one week and two weeks to do I was going to work not to work in the gym so much per se even though I did my heart was there to do this giant blackboard and then one day a member approached her with an opportunity that would change her life forever. A member had come in and said, okay, there's an apprenticeship going at Black Crown Tattoo Studio, which is the best tattoo studio in Shepparton. And this member would not take no for an answer. They're like, there's an apprenticeship, you have to do it. I'm sending it to you right now. I'm like, oh, but what happens if I get it? I'd worked at this job for nine and a half years. Like, what if I get it? And he's like, work that out then for now, just apply for it. So she applied. She put together a portfolio of all her different art mediums, including pictures of the chalkboards, and landed an interview. There was just one small problem. And at the time, I didn't actually have any tattoos. And I was sitting there and I was like, oh God, I have to say something. What am I going to say? And it's like, oh, okay. He goes, oh, that's all right. You can always get tattoo. So she got the apprenticeship at 38 with no tattoos and a chalkboard. But the apprenticeship was brutal, financially and emotionally. Kerri-Ann didn't know whether she would make it at first. Apprenticeships are never easy. You don't get a lot of money on any apprenticeships. When I first started, I was working for free. So $0 for tattoos, gaining some experience. And then you are charging the bare minimum. So then it was $50 for a tattoo. And then I think my half days were like $250, which is nothing. So to begin with, I was living off my savings. So as tough as it was for those few years, once you get through that, it just gets so much easier. But money wasn't actually the hardest part. The fear was. The biggest worry about getting into tattooing was making a mistake on someone and having that left with them forever. That played on my mind heavily, probably at least for the first 18 months. Every day I woke up, it was anxiety. I was very nervous. So how did she manage to get over that fear? The key to overcoming that fear and anxiety was persistence and just learning to be kinder to yourself. and the way that you speak to yourself is huge. Kerri-Ann is 41 now, a full-time tattoo artist at Black Crown Tattoo Studio. A lot of people ask her, do you wish you got into this sooner? Part of me says, yes, I would have loved to have done it sooner, but I definitely stand by that it was the right time to do it at that later stage in my life. You have more resilience being older, like I had children who I wouldn't have had the same time for. You were working in a studio, you were tattooing all day and then you were doing emails and designs outside of work hours. So it's a full, full-time job. So it's definitely not something I could have done any earlier in my life. So it was definitely the perfect time to like take that step as a more mature adult. A lot of people think changing careers is risky, especially later in life. But Kerri-Ann sees it the other way. A lot of people think it's like, you know, they're scared of that risk factor to change careers. But I actually think it's the opposite. it. I think it's a more riskier feeling to not take that chance and not follow your passion or follow your dream if that's what you're wanting because at the end of the day you've got one life and if you don't give it a go and do something that you're passionate about and you love then you've missed out. So just go for it.

So there's work like a career, and then there's stuff like your inner work, personal development, growth, that sort of thing. And it comes through seeking out environments where you're challenged and meeting people who teach you something new about the world. For Jacinta, public speaking was something she always found really hard and it was something that she had to work at. When I think about my biggest supporter, I think of my mum, Jacinta. She's always been the person in my corner, the one telling me I'm capable, important and allowed to take up space. It's a message everyone deserves to hear. It's a fact of life for every person. My mum never heard that message and without it, she was tasked with a strange kind of job, one that no one really teaches you. Put simply, Jacinta was tasked with learning to value herself. Hasn't it been overnight? It's been a slow, slow progress for me to build confidence in my own abilities and feel self-worth. Let's go back to 1982, where this process all began. Jacinta was a fresh Year 7 in high school. A new voluntary after-school activity had opened up at a high school. It was a public speaking course called Toastmasters. so you could do it um just as something to do um to increase your confidence with public speaking so my mum thought because of my um shyness she thought this would be good for me new school new beginning do this public speaking course and see how you go so I didn't particularly want to do it but Nana thought it was in her wisdom that it would be a good idea for me to do it was a bit hard to say no to nan in those days so would have thought oh well you know it sounds like something i'm going to have to do i'd absolutely dread the night of the um toastmasters course coming up like i'd feel sick and when it was my turn i'd stand up there be nervous feel the sweat trickling down my back i would literally just read off this piece of paper that I had written on like an essay and I could I'd do it as quickly as I possibly could to get it over and done with. I mean people say speak from the heart you'll be right which you can but then then you sort of think well you remember where you are you remember that you're standing up where everyone's looking at you focusing on what you are saying. The most ironic part of it all was that the one person encouraging Jacinta to do the course her mother was the very same person that influenced Jacinta to struggle with self-worth in the first place. Although there's a lot of love between me and my mum, she was probably not the most positive person in regards to helping me have confidence. She's always fault-finding, very little praise, very little praise. But we love each other, she's probably a product of her upbringing as well. without having the core foundations of feeling capable and enough an eight-week course aimed to build self-confidence was like an exercise of humiliation she didn't need hundreds of eyes watching her speak she just needed one person to tell her she was valuable like it didn't work it actually did the opposite effect because although you know if I did do this course what was the underlying issue I was still going on at home where I'd be you know I wasn't able to express myself in a way that was okay. It was always overridden and consequently that's happened in my future relationships as a result. The lack of external support Jacinta was given didn't just show up in moments like public speaking. It shaped the lens through which Jacinta navigated her entire life. Because I never believed in myself and I've only come to this realisation as an adult, like in the last, I don't know, maybe 10 years. If you can't believe in yourself, then you can't expect other people to believe in you. And I knew how debilitating it was in all aspects of growing up and living life, from career to family life to relationships. As life continued, Jacinta learnt that real confidence doesn't come from support. It comes from within. In a career as a nurse and experience through motherhood, self-worth was built through tangible results. Results that didn't just tell her she was capable or enough. They proved it to be true. At work I do get a lot of positive reinforcement like that is another part of my life where I feel very confident and capable in you know from the simplest thing of patients wanting to come back for me to give them their injections to I'll leave you in Jacinta's capable hands and all that sort of stuff so like and I never had that growing up never never never. The real measure of just how far Jacinta had come was when she did a speech at her father's 80th birthday in front of hundreds of people. I read out a nice speech and I spoke from the heart and although I wasn't I won't say I wasn't nervous I was but I was happy and proud of myself that I was actually able to do it and I actually volunteered to do it that no one said you know get up there and can you do um dad's speech I like I volunteered to do it so I think I was quite proud of myself in the end so for me I suppose that's a bit of an indication of how far I've come in regards to that so yeah it's taken a long time but I finally got there my mom's strength isn't loud and it never needed to be because real confidence was never about the room or who was watching it's something quieter a belief in your own worth that no one can ever really hand you and no one can take away

And I felt something, like this is it, like something clicked. He became an obsession. Gymnastics stopped being something he simply did after school. It became the center of his life. Every decision, every sacrifice, every thought somehow led back to the same dream. One day, standing under those lights himself. Then the day finally came. A cold morning in May, 500 athletes gathered inside the gym hall, all carrying the exact same hope while pretending not to be terrified. The first cut focused on routines. We already knew the routines. The coaches had put them online beforehand. We did the routines again and again. Until my feet didn't feel like mine anymore. But I made it through. By the end of the first cut, dozens had already been sent home. The second cut happened only hours later. Strength, endurance, physical suffering. This was where talent stopped mattering on its own. it's not something you can cheat with or run from either you're strong enough or you're not athletes collapsed onto the floor between exercises trying to catch their breath and slowly more people disappeared so i kept thinking about my six-year-old self and how much i did not want to disappoint him again so i didn't stop now there was only one thing left. The final cut. The jump. One moment capable of deciding everything. Hours, years, a childhood dream, all reduced to a few seconds in the air. I have never felt anything like it. I have never been that nervous. I could hear this sound, like buzzing, like bees inside my head. It became louder and louder. It felt like my veins inside my body was about to explode. my heart was pounding so hard my vision started closing in and I just told myself run I hit the mini tramp and then I land my spring and I'm standing perfect completely perfect I wasn't nervous anymore I was sure hours later everyone sat in a circle waiting for the final decision it was nearly two in the morning and then the coaches walked in one by one they started calling numbers. And with every number called, someone's dream either came true or disappeared. Number 10. Number 12. Number 11. Number 17. Number 19. And then my number never came up. It's like everything just stops. My body felt heavy, like I couldn't move. It was the biggest disappointment of my life. they just stole my dream but maybe that's the terrifying thing about dreams even when they destroy you they still refuse to leave because some dreams become too deeply rooted inside a person to disappear after one rejection or maybe five and maybe that's what separates people like from everyone else not talent not perfection but the willingness to stand back up after watching and your entire world collapse in front of you. I have thought about giving up a lot. After every rejection, there's a moment where you think, maybe this is it, maybe this is where it ends. But then I remember being six years old, standing there, looking up at them, feeling that thing in my chest. It's my dream. I can still feel it right here. So I keep going. I have to, but there's nothing else to do, but try again. Some dreams don't leave quietly. They stay. They follow you. They test how much pain you're willing to carry for them.
